title: Random Sampling
rights: Original teacher-authored practice; no AP Classroom materials or copied exam items.

items.prompt: A researcher selects 5 different names uniformly at random from a roster of 20, so that every possible five-person subset has equal chance. This is a
items.hint: The definition is about *all possible groups* of a fixed size.
items.solution: B. Every group of five has equal chance, precisely the definition of a simple random sample (SRS).
items.provenance: Maple Hill School authored original practice, October 2026

items.prompt: A fair app draws one student ID from 01–12, records it, returns it to the pool and repeats. Which result is possible?
items.hint: Ask whether a previously drawn ID was removed.
items.solution: C. Sampling *with replacement* restores the complete pool after each draw, so the same student ID may recur.
items.provenance: Maple Hill School authored original practice, October 2026

options.label: C
options.text: An ID may appear twice or more.

options.label: D
options.text: All 12 IDs must appear before any repeat.

items.prompt: A school has grades A, B and C. The researcher chooses a random sample of 10 students *within each grade* and combines them. Which design is this?
items.hint: Were *all* groups represented by within-group samples?
items.solution: D. Grades are the strata; a separate random sample is selected inside **each** grade.
items.provenance: Maple Hill School authored original practice, October 2026

items.prompt: A district randomly selects 4 of its 40 classrooms and surveys **every student** in the selected classrooms. Which design is this?
items.hint: What was randomly selected: whole classrooms or students within each classroom?
items.solution: A. Classrooms are clusters. An SRS of classrooms is chosen, and **all** their students are surveyed.
items.provenance: Maple Hill School authored original practice, October 2026

options.label: C
options.text: Simple random sample of individual students

items.prompt: There are 36 student IDs arranged in a list. A systematic sample of six uses an evenly spaced interval $k=N/n$. Find $k$.
items.hint: Divide population size by desired sample size.
items.solution: The interval is $k=36/6=\boxed{6}$. After a random starting position from 1 to 6, take every sixth ID.
items.provenance: Maple Hill School authored original practice, October 2026

items.prompt: An SRS of two students is drawn from six labelled students. How many distinct *unordered* two-person groups are possible?
items.hint: AB and BA are one group. Count 6 first choices and 5 second choices, then account for duplicate orderings.
items.provenance: Maple Hill School authored original practice, October 2026

items.prompt: Describe a valid SRS procedure for selecting six different students from a roster of 36. Include the labels, random device, and treatment of repeated labels.
items.hint: Specify the possible random integers and say exactly how you obtain six **distinct** labels.
items.solution: Number the rostered students 01–36. Use a random integer generator that assigns equal chance to 1 through 36. Keep each newly generated ID; reject repeated IDs and continue until six **distinct** IDs have been chosen. Survey those six students. Equivalently, shuffle all 36 IDs fairly and take the first six. This makes every unordered six-person subset equally likely.
items.provenance: Maple Hill School authored original practice, October 2026
items.rubric: Credit a complete eligible roster, uniformly random selection, unambiguous handling of repeats, and six distinct students. An arbitrary fixed list, first six volunteers or prechosen start is not an SRS.

items.prompt: The roster is grouped into six repeating blocks of six positions with grades A, B, C, A, B, C. A researcher uses systematic selection of every sixth name after a random start from 1 through 6. Explain one strength and one problem with this method.
items.hint: Compare equal chance of each *position* with the grades that appear in a given realized sample.
items.solution: The random start gives every roster position the same probability, $1/6$, of appearing and is fast to implement. However, all six selected positions share the same position in the repeating block and therefore all belong to the same grade. If travel time differs by grade, the sample may have high variability from one random start to another and give poor grade representation. The risk comes from the ordering pattern; a random start does not guarantee balance.
items.provenance: Maple Hill School authored original practice, October 2026
items.rubric: Identify both a legitimate procedural strength (random start, efficient, known inclusion pattern) and the systematic periodicity hazard linked explicitly to grade and the survey outcome. Do not claim that random systematic selection is always biased in one direction.

items.prompt: An orchard has 25 plots arranged in five rows from north to south. Explain how to choose a stratified random sample of five plots with one plot from *each row* using a random-number generator.
items.hint: A single sample of five plots from all 25 does not guarantee one from each row.
items.solution: Treat the five rows as distinct strata. Number the five plots in each row 1 through 5. Generate **one independent uniform random integer 1–5 in each row**, select the corresponding plot, and examine it. This produces exactly one selected plot per row, while each plot in a row has an equal selection chance.
items.provenance: Maple Hill School authored original practice, October 2026
items.rubric: Must specify rows as strata; select separately and independently within each row; use a clearly uniform mechanism from five plots; and collect one selected plot per row. Arbitrary choices or one SRS of five from the whole orchard do not satisfy the design.

items.prompt: A city needs average transit-wait times by neighbourhood, and residents of each neighbourhood vary substantially in age. Compare two options: (I) randomly select a few whole neighbourhoods and survey all their residents or (II) select a random set of residents *within every neighbourhood*. Recommend one for accurate neighbourhood-level summaries, naming both designs.
items.hint: Think about whether every neighbourhood contributes data.
items.solution: Option I is a **cluster sample** of neighbourhoods. It is cheaper when visiting whole neighbourhoods, but unsampled neighbourhoods supply no direct information, making neighbourhood-by-neighbourhood reporting impossible. Option II is a **stratified random sample**, with neighbourhoods as strata and separate random selections within each. It is better for neighbourhood-specific estimates because every neighbourhood contributes observations; sample sizes and weighting must be planned if estimating the whole city.
items.provenance: Maple Hill School authored original practice, October 2026
items.rubric: Correctly identify cluster and stratified sampling, recommend option II for comparisons by neighbourhood, and explain why each neighbourhood must contribute sampled residents. Cost tradeoffs and citywide weighting should be acknowledged if discussed.
